**Title:** Statin Initiation and Risk of Incident Alzheimer Disease and Cognitive Decline in Genetically Susceptible Older Adults.

**Authors:** Kumar B Rajan, Elizabeth A Mcaninch, Robert S Wilson, Anisa Dhana, Sara Evans-Lacko, Denis A Evans

**Journal:** Neurology
**Publication Date:** 2024-03-08
**DOI:** 10.1212/WNL.0000000000209168
**PMC ID:** 11770690
**Full Text Available:** Yes
**Full Text URL:** https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC11770690/


**Abstract:**
The association of statin initiation with incident Alzheimer disease (AD) dementia and cognitive decline by the APOE ε4 allele is unknown. Our objective was to examine whether the association of statin initiation with incident AD dementia and cognitive decline differs by the APOE ε4 allele.

The association of statin initiation with incident Alzheimer disease (AD) dementia and cognitive decline by the APOE ε4 allele is unknown. Our objective was to examine whether the association of statin initiation with incident AD dementia and cognitive decline differs by the APOE ε4 allele.

This population-based longitudinal cohort study was conducted in 4 urban communities in Chicago, IL, United States, consisting of 4,807 participants. Statin initiation is based on the inspection of medications during home assessments. Clinical diagnosis for incident AD used the NINCDS-ADRDA criteria, and longitudinal measurements of global cognition consisted of episodic memory, perceptual speed, and the Mini-Mental State Examination tests.

The study participants had a mean age of 72 years, consisting of 63% female individuals and 61% non-Hispanic Black individuals. During the study period, 1,470 (31%) participants reported statin initiation. In a covariate-adjusted competing risk model, statin initiation was associated with a reduced risk of incident clinical AD [hazard ratio (HR) 0.81 (95% CI 0.70–0.94)] compared with nonusers. This association was statistically significantly lower (p interaction = 0.015) among participants with the APOE ε4 allele [HR 0.60 (95% CI 0.49–0.74)] compared with those without the APOE ε4 allele [HR 0.96 (95% CI 0.82–1.12)]. The annual decline in global cognition (β = 0.021, 95% CI 0.007–0.034) and episodic memory (β = 0.020, 95% CI 0.007–0.033) was also substantially slower among participants with the APOE ε4 allele after statin initiation compared with nonusers. However, the association of statin initiation with cognitive decline was not significant among those without the APOE ε4 allele.

Our findings suggest that statins might be associated with a lower risk of incident AD among individuals with the APOE ε4 allele. The benefits of statin therapy need further consideration in randomized clinical trials, especially among those with the APOE ε4 allele.

This study provides Class II evidence that among those aged 65 years or older, statin initiation was associated with a reduced risk of Alzheimer disease, especially in the presence of an APOE-e4 allele.

Statin therapy in older adults is prevalent, with new guidelines addressing managing cholesterol levels and cardiovascular atherosclerosis disease.1 Abundant evidence supports the benefits of statin medications on cardiovascular disease,2 but the evidence for any perceived benefits for neurodegenerative diseases, such as Alzheimer disease (AD) and dementia, are mixed.3-13 The mechanism of how statin affects AD dementia and cognitive changes in old age, such as memory and executive functioning, is poorly understood. The high prevalence of statin use in the general population and its potential benefits on AD dementia make this a topic of high public health significance.

Elevated levels of blood cholesterol can lead to damage in the blood vessels of the brain, potentially resulting in decreased blood flow.14 The reduced cerebral blood flow could contribute to an increased risk of stroke and high susceptibility to dementia.15,16 Although hyperlipidemia in mid-life is associated with an increased risk of dementia in old age,17,18 a relatively high fraction of older adults develop hyperlipidemia in old age,19 and little is known on how late-life statin initiation may be related to dementia risk. Besides advanced age, another well-established risk factor of AD dementia is a cholesterol transport–coding protein, the APOE, and carriers of the APOE ε4 allele also have a significantly elevated risk of AD dementia.20-22 Whether statin use modifies the association of the APOE ε4 allele association with AD dementia is not well-defined, with some studies suggesting benefit,10 while others show no benefit.9 While statin use decreases the risk of all-cause mortality,23 particularly the reduced risk of cardiovascular disease (CVD) mortality in mid-life,24 the benefits of late-life statin initiation on all-cause mortality and CVD mortality are also not established.

The goals of this study are to test whether statin initiation in older age is associated with a reduced risk of AD dementia among those with and without the APOE ε4 allele and to examine whether statin initiation is associated with a slower decline in global and individual tests of cognition among participants with and without the APOE ε4 allele. As a secondary outcome, we also examined the association of statin initiation with all-cause mortality and total CVD mortality and test whether this association differs by the APOE ε4 allele.

The Chicago Health and Aging Project (CHAP) is a population-based longitudinal study that examined the epidemiology of Alzheimer disease and was performed between 1993 and 2012 in 4 urban neighborhoods in the South side of Chicago.25 Approximately 79% of adults identified older than 65 years agreed to participate in the study following a door-to-door census performed in 1993. During subsequent years, adults who attained the age of 65 years were also enrolled as successive cohorts for replenishment. The CHAP data were collected in triennial cycles, with the original cohort starting in 1993 and subsequent cycles in 1997, 2000, 2003, 2006, and 2009. New replenishment cohorts were included starting from the 2000 data collection period, with 6 cycles of population interviews being performed. In a third of each population cycle, a stratified random sample was chosen for clinical diagnosis of AD dementia, during which DNA samples were extracted (Figure 1).

AD = Alzheimer disease; DNA = deoxyribonucleic acid.

Of the 9,321 eligible statin nonusers at baseline, the APOE genotyping was performed on 4,807 (52%) participants. We used sampling weights based on demographic characteristics to account for the selection probability for clinical evaluation of incident AD dementia and DNA extraction. Participants with DNA samples were similar in age, sex, race/ethnicity, and cognitive functioning to those without DNA samples. In addition, during follow-up, a total of 4,655 (50%) participants died, and the mortality rate was not different by the APOE ε4 allele.

At the end of each population interview, a stratified random sample based on age, sex, race/ethnicity, and cognitive level was selected for clinical evaluation of incident AD dementia. Clinical evaluations were structured and uniform, with neurologists blinded to population interview cognitive testing and stratified sampling categories.26 Clinical evaluations included a structured medical history, neurologic examination, and 19 neurocognitive tests. Unaware of previously collected data, a board-certified neurologist diagnosed AD and dementia according to the National Institute of Neurological and Communicative Disorders and Stroke and the Alzheimer Disease and Related Disorders Association criteria.27 A clinical diagnosis of AD dementia required a history of cognitive decline and evidence of impairment in 2 or more cognitive domains. In our study, 1,928 participants were clinically evaluated for incident AD dementia, and 550 (29%) had multiple clinical evaluations.

Every 3 years, during the population interviews, a short battery of cognitive tests was administered to study participants. This short battery consisted of tests for episodic memory using delayed and immediate story recalls,28,29 a test for executive function using a Symbol Digit Modalities Test,30 and a global test of orientation and cognition using the Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE).31 A global cognitive function test score was created by centering and scaling each test score because 75% of the variability in the test scores was explained by a single factor.32 We computed z scores for each test based on the baseline mean values and standard deviations for the entire CHAP sample. We then calculated a composite z score by averaging the z scores from all 4 tests. A positive z score reflects better cognitive performance compared with the average for the population, while a negative score indicates lower cognitive function. The raw test scores were skewed and had high ceiling floor effects. However, standardizing the tests ensures a normal distribution and reduces the ceiling floor effects.

Our ascertainment of mortality was completed through December 31, 2012. The primary source of death data was the Social Security Administration Death Master File, supplemented by field contacts with family and neighbors. Beginning from January 1, 2008, the National Death Index (NDI Plus) reports confirmed 1,672 (80%) deceased. Of the remaining participants, an additional 188 (9%) died after 1/1/2013, with confirmation dependent on the release of later versions of the NDI database. Only 242 (11%) could not be confirmed due to a lack of personal identifiers. Our sample size for all-cause mortality included all 4,807 participants with the APOE ε4 allele.

Total CVD mortality was based on death classifications in NDI Plus, where ICD-9 classification codes 390–459 or ICD-10 I00-I99 were used only among participants with NDI-confirmed deaths. To supplement our mortality data, we classified participants in our Medicare data who died within 3 years of a cardiovascular event as total CVD-related mortality.33 In our sample, 4,227 (88%) participants were ascertained as total CVD mortality based on NDI Plus and the remaining 580 (12%) using 3-year cardiovascular events in the Medicare database.

At each in-home population interview, participants provided their medication information for direct inspection over the preceding 2 weeks. The labels of medications were recorded and classified using the MediSpan system,34 Wolters Kluwer Clinical Drug Information, which facilitated the grouping of medications by biologically active agents. Medications were classified into various categories, including statin (simvastatin, atorvastatin, pravastatin, fluvastatin, cerivastatin, and lovastatin). In our study, 1,470 participants reported initiation of statin use during follow-up ascertainments, while 1,481 participants reported statin use during the baseline visit. Due to the advantages of the initiator approach in observational studies,35 we focused on 2 groups of individuals—initiators and nonusers—and removed current users at baseline from our analysis. A time-dependent variable was created for participants who initiated statin medication use during the follow-up period vs those who never used statin medications.

The APOE ε4 genotypes were determined by rs7412 and rs429358 single-nucleotide variations (SNVs). We performed the genotyping at the Broad Institute for Population Genetics using the hME Sequenom MassARRAY platform. The genotyping process yielded a 100% call rate for SNV rs7412 and a 99.8% call rate for SNV rs429358. In addition, we observed that both SNVs adhered to Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, with corresponding p values of 0.0833 and 0.7925, respectively. Using these 2 SNVs, we established an indicator variable to identify participants carrying 1 or more copies of the APOE ε4 allele.

We estimated the sample weight–adjusted grouped mean values and 95% confidence intervals for baseline age, education, global and individual cognitive test scores, and proportions for race/ethnicity, sex, the APOE ε4 allele, and history of health characteristics stratified by nonusers and initiators. We compared these characteristics using a generalized linear model after adjusting for sampling weight using an identity or logit link function depending on the nature of measurement.

A competing risk illness-death model with time-dependent statin initiation was used to estimate the risk of incident AD dementia, with death as a competing risk in individuals not diagnosed with incident AD dementia. The cumulative incidence function is a probability subdistribution function from a specific failure cause. We used the Fine and Gray extension of the Cox regression that models the hazards of the cumulative incidence function.38 The APOE ε4 allele stratified the competing risk model; 2 separate models were performed in those with and without the APOE ε4 allele. The difference in the association of time-dependent statin initiation with incident AD dementia was tested using the interaction of the APOE ε4 allele with statin initiation. A covariate-adjusted Kaplan-Meir curve was used to examine the difference in survival function for overall mortality and total CVD mortality between time-dependent statin initiation and nonusers. The competing risk model, cumulative incidence function, and Kaplan-Meir curves were fitted in SAS software.39

A joint model for longitudinal changes in cognitive function and time to mortality was used to account for mortality bias in older adults.40 The linear mixed-effects component was used to estimate the differences between statin initiators and nonusers in average levels and the annual decline in cognitive function. The longitudinal model for cognitive decline was based on a time-dependent measure of statin initiation to examine cognitive decline before and after statin initiation using a linear mixed-effects model. Given that almost 50% of participants died during the study follow-up, we accounted for mortality using a time-to-event model to account for truncation by estimating the parameters of the longitudinal model and time-to-mortality model within a shared parameter model framework.41 The joint models were performed separately in those with and without the APOE ε4 allele and adjusted for sampling weights for selection to the DNA sample. Four models—global cognition and 3 individual tests of cognition were fitted using this approach, allowing for random effects for person-specific levels and person-specific slopes after adjusting for age, sex, race/ethnicity, education, and interaction of time since baseline or statin initiation with the 4 demographic variables. Joint models were fitted using the JM library with LME and survival function in the R program.42 All statistical tests used the nominal significance of 5% type I error rates.

The Rush University Medical Center Institutional Review Board approved population interviews, clinical evaluations, and DNA extraction for this study before participant enrollment. Written signed informed consent was obtained from all participants in the study.

Deidentified participant data will be shared upon approval of a data request proposal and data use agreement with the requesting institution and investigators. Study materials and protocols will be made available up to 1 year from the publication and request of the deidentified data.

The study consisted of 4,807 participants, aged on average 72 years, with no statin use and no prevalent AD at baseline (Table 1). Of those participants, 1,470 (30.6%) initiated statin therapy during the study. Individuals who initiated statin therapy (i.e., statin initiators) were younger than nonusers and had higher global cognition, episodic memory, executive function, and MMSE scores than nonusers despite the same level of education (Table 1). Participants had a higher prevalence of the APOE ε4 allele in statin initiators (39%) than nonusers (32%), p = 0.01. Statin initiators were also more likely to have prevalent heart disease (13%) than nonusers (9%), p = 0.02. We found no significant differences in race/ethnicity, sex, and history of diabetes and stroke between statin initiators and nonusers.

The median study years was 9.8 years, with 47,583 person-years of follow-up. The average time from baseline assessment to statin initiation was 6.9 years (Table 1), and the average time from statin initiation to clinical diagnosis of incident AD dementia was 4.2 years. During the follow-up, the incidence of AD dementia was lower among statin initiators (17%) compared with that among nonusers (23%), a statistically significant difference (p value = 0.035).

Over time, incident AD was assessed in 4 subgroups of participants by statin initiation, nonuse, and APOE ε4 allele carrier/noncarrier status (Figure 2) in a sample weight model adjusted for demographic and health characteristics. Among participants with the APOE ε4 allele, the cumulative incidence of AD after statin initiation (blue) was significantly lower than that of APOE ε4 carriers not taking any statin medication (green). Among participants without the APOE ε4 allele, the cumulative incidence function of incident AD dementia after statin initiation (brown) and noncarriers not taking statin medication (red) overlapped, with no overt visual difference between the 2 curves. Strikingly, the cumulative incidence function of participants with the APOE ε4 with a statin (blue) initiation overlapped with that of participants without the APOE ε4 allele (red and brown). The subgroup of participants with the APOE ε4 allele and without statin use (green) experienced the most incident AD (Figure 2).

APOE = Apolipoprotein E.

Using a covariate and sample weight–adjusted competing risk model, we found that time-dependent statin initiation was associated with a 19% lower risk of incident AD dementia (HR 0.81, 95% CI 0.70–0.94; Figure 3, top panel). Stratified by APOE ε4 allele, the association of statin initiation and AD risk was significantly lower among participants with the APOE ε4 allele (HR 0.60, 95% CI 0.49–0.74) than that among those without the APOE ε4 allele (HR 0.96, 95% 0.82–1.12, p interaction = 0.015). No racial differences in the association of statin initiation with incident AD dementia between African Americans and European Americans were observed (p = 0.38).

AD = Alzheimer disease; APOE = Apolipoprotein E; CVD = cardiovascular disease. The bars around the hazard ratios are 95% confidence intervals. Hazard ratios adjusted for demographic and chronic health conditions are presented for all participants and those with and without the APOE ε4 allele.

The covariate-adjusted Kaplan-Meir survival curves for overall and total CVD mortality for time-dependent statin initiation and those not taking statin medications are shown in Figure 4. Participants with statin initiation in old age had a lower probability of overall mortality and total CVD mortality (red line) than nonusers (black line). Using a Cox regression model, statin initiation was also associated with reduced risk of overall mortality (HR, 0.82, 95% CI 0.74–0.91; Figure 3, middle) and total CVD mortality (HR, 0.64, 95% CI 0.55–0.74; Figure 3, bottom). The association of statin initiation with overall mortality and total CVD mortality was not statistically different between those with and without the APOE ε4 allele.

CVD = cardiovascular disease. Mortality based on National Death Index with red line for statin initiators and black line for nonusers.

Using a joint model for longitudinal change in cognition, participants with the APOE ε4 allele showed a significantly slower decline in global cognition after statin initiation compared with nonusers, a slower annual decline of 0.021 standard deviation units per year (Table 2). Among participants without the APOE ε4 allele, we found no significant difference between statin initiators and nonusers on the annual change in global cognition (p = 0.059). A similar pattern of change was observed for the annual change in episodic memory and MMSE. Among participants with the APOE ε4 allele, statin initiation was associated with a slower annual decline in episodic memory and MMSE. However, statin initiation was not associated with the annual decline in episodic memory and MMSE among participants without the APOE ε4 allele (Table 3). Statin initiation was not associated with the annual change in executive functioning among APOE ε4 allele carriers and noncarriers (Table 3).

We also found that statin initiators had a higher baseline cognitive functioning than nonusers among those without the APOE ε4 allele. However, this difference was not significant among those with the APOE ε4 allele. We also performed additional sensitivity analysis, including physical activities and body mass index, but did not see any change in our findings, estimates, or overall conclusions.

Statin initiation in old age is associated with a low risk of incident AD dementia among participants with the APOE ε4 allele. In noncarriers of the APOE ε4 allele, statin use was not associated with the risk of AD dementia. The potential interaction of statin initiation and the APOE ε4 allele on the risk of incident AD dementia is appealing because the presence of the APOE ε4 allele increases the genetic susceptibility of AD dementia. These findings were further supported by the results of statin use and cognitive domains, especially episodic memory. This finding is significant because a clinical diagnosis of AD dementia depends on memory loss as one of the 2 impaired cognitive domains.27 While promising, these findings should be cautiously interpreted and further tested in other population-based studies and, ultimately, in clinical trials.

The consistency of our findings that statin initiation in old age might be associated with slower cognitive decline and reduced risk of incident AD dementia gives a higher level of confidence than this being an isolated finding. APOE is an apolipoprotein that plays an essential role in cholesterol transport. In the brain, cholesterol is transmitted from astrocytes to neurons through lipoprotein particles, where APOE is a primary component.43 Recent studies provide evidence that abnormal cholesterol metabolism by ApoE4 could be linked to AD pathology.44-46 Regarding cholesterol-lowering medications, a pooled analysis of 36 studies47 showed that statins were associated with a decreased risk of dementia (OR 0.80 [CI 0.75–0.86]) and AD (21 studies, OR 0.68 [CI 0.56–0.81]). The cholesterol protein–coding mechanism through the APOE ε4 allele and statin initiation to treat hyperlipidemia might have some overlapping mechanism that might translate to reducing the risk of incident AD dementia and cognitive decline. Another study evaluated the effects of withdrawal or continuation of statins in people with dementia on cognitive outcomes.48 They selected all randomized controlled clinical trials with either a placebo or “no treatment” control group. They found no studies suitable for inclusion; therefore, the authors did not analyze any data. Eventually, randomized controlled studies need to be conducted to assess the cognitive outcomes of statins in participants with dementia. In terms of statins, another study tested whether statin use is associated with an increased or decreased risk of dementia after a concussion.49 The authors concluded that in older adults, the risk of dementia after a concussion was associated with a modest reduction among patients receiving a statin.

The relation of statin initiation on cognitive decline is also novel and has not been previously reported by the APOE ε4 allele. Given the potential late-life effect of the APOE ε4 allele on the risk of incident AD and cognitive decline,22 the relevance of statin initiation in possibly partially slowing the rapid cognitive decline makes this a topic of high significance. One of the strengths of the study is the use of a population sample rather than a clinical setting, so adjusting for demographic and health confounders was more feasible. The population-based statin initiation was roughly 30% during follow-up and was similar to other estimates of statin use in older populations.6 Our focus was on individuals initiating statin medication in late life. These individuals reported a higher prevalence of heart disease and a similar history of diabetes and stroke but a lower risk of AD dementia during follow-up. The time from statin initiation to clinical diagnosis of AD dementia was 4.2 years, which surprisingly overlaps with the time of cognitive inflection before developing AD dementia,50 making statin initiation a measure of potential interest for future clinical trials. Several limitations also need to be noted. Our work is focused on incident AD dementia, and removing individuals with lower cognitive function is likely to bias our findings. However, after adjusting for selection bias, the similarity in education, an indicator of socioeconomic status suggests that statin initiation did not depend on economic status. Hence, our estimates provide a consistent risk estimate even after accounting for the APOE sample selection.

Given the small sample size in each subcategory of statin medication, especially by the APOE ε4 allele carrier status, we could not examine the association of statin medication subtypes with incident AD dementia or cognitive decline. We also did not assess the association between other lipid-lowering agents and AD dementia because the number of participants taking non-statin lipid-lowering medications was low. We did not collect cholesterol at baseline and could not test whether cholesterol levels mediated the association between statin treatment and decreased risk of AD dementia. Although we inspected the pill bottles, it is unclear whether the participants were taking the medication (or were adherent). Approximately 6% of individuals with statin initiation did not take statin medications in the next cycle. The reason for discontinuity in the statin medication is not apparent, with one of the issues being statin intolerance. Removing these individuals did not change our results or conclusions. However, these issues might interest future epidemiologic studies or meta-analyses of epidemiologic studies.

Our findings show that statin initiation in older age was significantly associated with a reduced risk of incident AD dementia after accounting for death as a competing event. This risk reduction was more prominent among the APOE ε4 allele carriers, a gene strongly associated with an increased risk of AD dementia. Given the possible protective effects of statin initiation, particularly among those with the APOE ε4 allele, this is a high potential public health significance finding. Even if these associations do not meet the incident AD dementia threshold, there is evidence in our population suggesting that statin initiation may slow the decline in cognition and, more importantly, the decline in episodic memory among those with the APOE ε4 allele.
